outline.description: This opening chapter motivates the problem addressed by the paper: learning accurate predictive models from very small tabular datasets. It introduces why tabular learning matters in practice, why few-shot settings are difficult, and why large language models may offer a new source of prior knowledge.
subtopics: What tabular learning is and why it is central in domains such as healthcare and finance
The few-shot setting: limited labels, high variance, and risk of overfitting
Why standard supervised tabular models struggle with very small training sets
The value of prior knowledge when labeled data are scarce
How large language models encode broad world knowledge that may help tabular prediction
The paper's core question: can LLMs act as feature engineers instead of end-to-end predictors?

outline.chapter_title: 2. Background: Existing Approaches to Few-Shot Tabular Learning
outline.description: This chapter places the paper in context by reviewing the main families of methods that came before it. It helps students understand what problem FeatLLM is trying to solve more effectively than prior approaches.
subtopics: Conventional tabular baselines: logistic regression, random forests, and gradient-boosted trees
Semi-supervised and self-supervised methods for tabular data
Why augmentation and pretraining are harder for heterogeneous tabular features than for images or text
Transfer learning for tables: TransTab, TabPFN, and related ideas
Language-interfaced tabular learning through serialization of tables into text
In-context learning for tabular tasks
Parameter-efficient tuning approaches such as LoRA and IA3
Representative LLM-tabular systems: TabLLM, TABLET, and related methods
Key limitations of prior LLM-based methods: per-sample inference cost, fine-tuning requirements, and prompt length constraints

outline.description: This chapter presents the conceptual leap of the paper. Instead of asking an LLM to directly classify every test sample, FeatLLM asks the LLM to infer reusable rules that can be turned into features and then fed into a simple classifier.
subtopics: From black-box prediction to explicit feature engineering
Using LLMs to infer criteria or rules associated with each class
Why rule discovery can be cheaper than end-to-end LLM inference at test time
Separation of responsibilities: LLM for knowledge extraction, simple model for prediction
How this design enables API-only usage without model fine-tuning
How the approach reduces inference latency and avoids repeated LLM queries for every sample
How bagging helps address long prompts and large feature sets
Overview of the full FeatLLM pipeline from prompts to final ensemble predictions

outline.description: This chapter formalizes the learning problem solved by FeatLLM and clarifies the assumptions needed by the method, including feature metadata and the few-shot classification setting.
subtopics: Formal definition of the labeled tabular dataset
Input features, feature names, and feature descriptions in natural language
Classification as the target setting, including binary and multiclass tasks
The k-shot protocol and how training examples are sampled
The importance of column names, types, and definitions for language-based reasoning
The distinction between raw tabular inputs and generated rule-based features

outline.chapter_title: 5. Prompting an LLM to Extract Predictive Rules
outline.description: This chapter explains the prompt engineering strategy at the heart of FeatLLM. It teaches how the system structures prompts so the LLM can reason about the task, connect features to labels, and output rules in a usable format.
subtopics: Why prompt design matters for reliable rule extraction
The three parts of the prompt: basic information, reasoning instruction, and response instruction
Task descriptions as natural-language questions
Feature descriptions, value types, and category examples
Few-shot demonstrations and the serialization of tabular rows into text
The serialization template for sample-label pairs
Two-step reasoning instruction for rule generation
Step 1: inferring likely causal relationships or tendencies using prior knowledge
Step 2: using few-shot examples plus prior knowledge to derive class-specific rules
How the two-step design aims to reduce reliance on spurious correlations
Why the model is asked to generate a fixed number of rules per class
Response formatting instructions for easier downstream parsing
Handling different feature types when expressing rules
The role of chain-of-thought-style guidance in improving reasoning quality

outline.chapter_title: 6. Turning Natural-Language Rules into Machine-Usable Features
outline.description: After the LLM outputs rules, FeatLLM must transform them into executable logic. This chapter explains the parsing challenge and the paper's distinctive choice to use the LLM itself to generate parsing code.
subtopics: Why natural-language rules cannot be used directly by standard classifiers
The challenge of noisy syntax in LLM outputs
Examples of equivalent but differently phrased conditions such as symbolic versus verbal inequalities
Why brittle hand-built parsers are difficult to maintain
Using an LLM as a semantic parser and code generator
Prompting the LLM with function signatures, input-output descriptions, and rules
Generating Python code that checks whether a sample satisfies each rule
Executing generated code with Python exec() to transform data
Constructing binary features that mark whether each rule is satisfied
Benefits and risks of code generation in a learning pipeline

outline.chapter_title: 7. Predicting Class Probabilities from Rule-Based Features
outline.description: This chapter shows how FeatLLM converts the generated binary features into final predictions using a very simple downstream model. It also explains why learning rule importance matters even when rules are informative.
subtopics: Why counting satisfied rules is a natural starting point
Why simple counting is insufficient when rules vary in usefulness
Class-specific binary feature vectors for rule satisfaction
The linear model used to score each class
The non-negative weight constraint and its interpretation
Computing logits through weighted sums of satisfied rules
Applying softmax to obtain class probabilities
Optimizing cross-entropy loss with few-shot labeled data
Learning which rules are most important for each class
Why the downstream model remains simple despite LLM-generated features
Interpretability of learned weights over rules

outline.chapter_title: 8. Ensembling, Bagging, and Managing Prompt Length
outline.description: This chapter explains the robustness mechanisms of FeatLLM. It covers how the method repeatedly generates rule sets and combines them, and why bagging is both a statistical tool and a practical solution to prompt-size limitations.
subtopics: Why a single LLM-generated rule set may be noisy or incomplete
Repeated rule extraction across multiple trials
Using non-determinism in LLM sampling through temperature
Randomizing the order of few-shot demonstrations
Feature bagging and instance bagging in the prompt construction process
Training multiple weak learners and averaging their predicted probabilities
Connections to ensemble learning and random forests
Self-consistency intuition: rules repeated across trials are more likely to be reliable
How bagging helps when the table has too many features or examples for one prompt
Trade-offs between diversity, coverage, and computational budget

outline.chapter_title: 9. Experimental Design: Datasets, Baselines, and Implementation
outline.description: This chapter teaches how the authors evaluated FeatLLM and why the experimental protocol is appropriate for few-shot tabular learning. It also provides the practical setup needed to reproduce the method.
subtopics: Overview of the 13 evaluation datasets and their task diversity
Classic tabular benchmarks: Adult, Bank, Blood, Car, Communities, Credit-g, Diabetes, Heart, and Myocardial
Recently added or synthetic datasets: Cultivars, NHANES, Sequence-type, and Solution-mix
Why recent and synthetic datasets matter for testing memorization concerns
Binary versus multiclass evaluation settings
Baselines from conventional machine learning
Baselines using unlabeled data: SCARF and STUNT
Transfer-pretrained baseline: TabPFN
LLM-based baselines: in-context learning, TABLET, and TabLLM
Choice of LLM backbone: GPT-3.5 for FeatLLM
Why TabLLM cannot use GPT-3.5 in the original setup
Key implementation settings: temperature, top-p, ensemble count, and rules per class
Optimization details for the linear model using Adam
Cross-validation and hyperparameter selection
Evaluation metric: AUC and repeated runs with different train-test randomness

outline.description: This chapter presents the central findings of the paper and teaches students how to interpret them. It focuses on comparative performance, data efficiency, and practical advantages over prior LLM-based systems.
subtopics: Performance of FeatLLM across all datasets
Average improvement over alternatives such as TabLLM and STUNT
Cases where FeatLLM ranks first or second among baselines
Few-shot efficiency: 4-shot FeatLLM compared with 32-shot conventional methods
Performance on datasets with many features where prompt length is challenging
Why some LLM baselines fail on high-dimensional tables
Advantages of not requiring per-sample LLM inference at test time
Interpreting performance variability across domains and datasets
What the results suggest about LLM prior knowledge as a source of useful tabular features

outline.description: This chapter dissects the method to identify which components matter most and why. It also covers the paper's diagnostic experiments on efficiency, feature quality, spurious correlations, and hyperparameters.
subtopics: Ablation of weight tuning versus simple rule counting
Ablation of ensemble averaging
Ablation of feature descriptions in the prompt
Ablation of the first reasoning step based on prior knowledge
How the contribution of each component changes with the number of shots
Training-time and inference-time comparison with other methods
Why FeatLLM's inference cost is closer to standard tabular models than to other LLM methods
Measuring the informativeness of generated features using AUROC
Ratio of useful rules before and after linear-model tuning
How tuning filters weak or irrelevant rules through learned weights
Robustness to spurious correlations by adding unrelated columns
Why the reasoning stage helps ignore irrelevant features
Limits of this robustness when unrelated columns come from closely related domains
Hyperparameter analysis for number of ensembles

Performance trade-offs among prompt length, feature dimensionality, diversity, and overfitting

outline.chapter_title: 12. Limitations, Broader Impact, and Future Directions
outline.description: The final chapter helps students critically assess the paper. It summarizes the method's strengths, discusses its limitations and societal implications, and outlines promising next research steps.
subtopics: Why FeatLLM is especially designed for low-shot learning rather than large-data regimes
Dependence on feature names and natural-language descriptions
Potential brittleness in rule generation and code execution
Biases and misinformation embedded in LLM prior knowledge
Risks in sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance
Interpretability benefits and their current limits
Why API-only access makes the method practical for modern closed LLMs
Future work on richer feature types beyond rules
Extending the framework to larger datasets and broader task families
Improving interpretability, reliability, and safety of LLM-assisted feature engineering
Final synthesis: what FeatLLM contributes to the evolution of tabular machine learning
